summary: Easy: any GitHub account can register an OAuth app now, with no provider review or payment, so you can connect your own account as soon as setup is done. The gate that most limits launch is organization approval: if a user's organization restricts OAuth apps, its members cannot connect until an organization owner approves your app.
timeToProduction: Immediate for users on personal accounts. Members of restricted organizations wait until the organization owner approves the app, a wait GitHub does not time.

gates.title: Any GitHub account can register the app
gates.what: You can register the app under your personal account or under any organization where you have admin access. No business account, partner status or paid plan is required. Each user or organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps.
gates.where: Settings > Developer settings > OAuth apps > New OAuth App. You act here.
gates.todo: Register the app under the account that should own it, since ownership is hard to move later.

gates.title: No separate test mode before launch
gates.what: No sandbox or test mode is documented for OAuth apps. Test by connecting your own account to the app.

gates.title: No provider review for a basic OAuth app
gates.what: Registering an OAuth app involves no review or verification step in the docs. Marketplace listing has its own requirements, but it is optional for connecting users.

gates.title: Organization owners may need to approve your app
gates.what: If a user's organization has OAuth app access restrictions enabled, its members cannot authorize your app against organization resources. They can request approval, and owners are notified.
gates.where: Organization Settings > Third-party access > OAuth app policy. The organization owner acts here, not you.
gates.todo: Tell users in restricted organizations that their owner must approve the app. Keep your app's description accurate, since owners review it.

gates.title: No paid plan needed to use the API
gates.what: Connecting users and calling the API does not require a paid plan. A higher rate limit exists only for apps owned or approved by a GitHub Enterprise Cloud organization.

gates.title: Access tokens expire by default and rate limits are per user
gates.what: Expiring user access tokens are enabled by default, so tokens last eight hours and come with a refresh token. Each user's requests count against their own 5,000 requests per hour. Rate-limit increases are granted per app.
gates.where: App settings > Expire user access tokens checkbox. You act here.
gates.todo: Implement refresh-token handling before launch. Watch for rate-limit responses, and do not retry until the reset time.

requirements.text: A GitHub account, or an organization where you have admin access, to own the app.
A public homepage URL and at least one authorization callback URL.
A privacy-safe app name and description, since everything you enter is public.

steps.text: Open Settings > Developer settings > OAuth apps in your GitHub account or organization.
steps.detail: Use the account that should own the app.

steps.text: Click New OAuth App and enter the application name, homepage URL and authorization callback URL.
steps.detail: Callback URL is where users return after approval. You can add up to 10 callback URLs.

steps.text: Leave Enable Device Flow unchecked unless the app runs on a CLI, IoT device or headless system.
steps.detail: Device flow lets attackers impersonate the app in phishing, so it should stay off for web apps.

steps.text: Keep Expire user access tokens checked unless your authentication code cannot yet handle short-lived tokens.
steps.detail: If you must uncheck it, do so only until refresh-token support is added.

steps.text: Click Register application and store the client secret in a secure secret store.
steps.detail: Never put the client secret in client-side code or code on user devices.

steps.text: Draft the setup text users will see when approving the app, including a note about organization approval.
steps.detail: Keep it factual: name the data the app accesses and the scopes it requests.

steps.text: Connect your own account to the app end to end, including token refresh.
steps.detail: Test from a personal account and from an organization you administer.

steps.text: Ask organization owners in restricted organizations to approve the app.
steps.detail: Owners act in their organization's OAuth app policy. Their response time is not controlled by GitHub.

steps.text: Launch and share the client ID with users.

blockers.problem: Members of a restricted organization get an error or cannot authorize the app.
blockers.fix: Have the organization owner approve the app under Third-party access > OAuth app policy.

blockers.problem: Client secret is exposed in a public repo or front-end code.
blockers.fix: Rotate the secret, update your app, and delete the old one. Keep the secret server-side only.

blockers.problem: Users are logged out after eight hours because refresh is not implemented.
blockers.fix: Store the refresh token and exchange it for a new access token before expiry.

blockers.problem: Rate-limit errors appear because your app shares the user's 5,000 requests per hour with their other tools.
blockers.fix: Pace requests using the x-ratelimit headers and back off on 403 or 429 responses.

blockers.problem: Device flow enabled on a web app allows phishing against your users.
blockers.fix: Turn off Enable Device Flow in the app settings.

couldNotVerify: Exact time an organization owner takes to approve an app; GitHub does not state this.
Whether a new OAuth app's organization restriction default applies to every organization, as the official pages do not state it.

claims.statement: Any user can create and register an OAuth app under a personal account or an organization where they have administrative access.
claims.sourceTitle: Creating an OAuth app - GitHub Docs
claims.quote: You can create and register an OAuth app under your personal account or under any organization you have administrative access to.

claims.statement: A user or organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps.
claims.sourceTitle: Creating an OAuth app - GitHub Docs
claims.quote: A user or organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps.

claims.statement: No sandbox or test mode is mentioned in Creating an OAuth app - GitHub Docs.
claims.sourceTitle: Creating an OAuth app - GitHub Docs
claims.note: Absence claim from the registration page.

claims.statement: No app review or verification step is mentioned in Creating an OAuth app - GitHub Docs.
claims.sourceTitle: Creating an OAuth app - GitHub Docs
claims.note: Absence claim from the registration page. Marketplace listing has a separate review and is not required.

claims.statement: When an organization has OAuth app access restrictions enabled, its members cannot authorize the app against organization resources until an owner approves it.
claims.sourceTitle: About OAuth app access restrictions - GitHub Docs
claims.quote: When OAuth app access restrictions are enabled, organization members and outside collaborators cannot authorize OAuth app access to organization resources.

claims.statement: No paid plan is mentioned as required for OAuth app API access in Creating an OAuth app - GitHub Docs.
claims.sourceTitle: Creating an OAuth app - GitHub Docs
claims.note: Absence claim from the registration page.

claims.statement: Expiring user access tokens are enabled by default for new OAuth apps.
claims.sourceTitle: Creating an OAuth app - GitHub Docs
claims.quote: Expire user access tokens is enabled by default.

claims.statement: With expiring tokens, the access token expires after eight hours and the refresh token expires after six months.
claims.sourceTitle: Best practices for creating an OAuth app - GitHub Docs
claims.quote: The access token expires after eight hours, and the refresh token expires after six months.

claims.statement: Requests made with an OAuth app's tokens count against the authorizing user's personal limit of 5,000 requests per hour.
claims.sourceTitle: Rate limits for the REST API - GitHub Docs
claims.quote: All of these requests count towards your personal rate limit of 5,000 requests per hour.

claims.statement: Device flow should stay disabled unless the app runs in a constrained environment, because it can be used for phishing.
claims.sourceTitle: Best practices for creating an OAuth app - GitHub Docs
claims.quote: For this reason, do not enable the device flow for your application unless you are using the app in a constrained environment (CLIs, IoT devices, or headless systems).

claims.statement: The client secret and generated tokens must be stored securely.
claims.sourceTitle: Best practices for creating an OAuth app - GitHub Docs
claims.quote: You must store your app's client secret and any generated tokens securely, if possible.

claims.statement: Only public information should be used in the OAuth app's name, URLs and description.
claims.sourceTitle: Creating an OAuth app - GitHub Docs
claims.quote: Only use information in your OAuth app that you consider public.

claims.statement: Rate-limit increases are granted per OAuth app, and every token granted to that app gets the increased limit.
claims.sourceTitle: Differences between GitHub Apps and OAuth apps - GitHub Docs
claims.quote: Rate limit increases are granted per OAuth app.

claims.statement: Time to test and effort estimates are approximate, based on the registration steps.
